in_text_mentions: gins locally and is limited to the soft tissues around the erupting tooth. Patients usually describe it as pulsating and eventually radiating to the surrounding tissues and/or distant areas (soft palate, mouth floor, retromandibular and submandibular space, throat, ear, or temporomandibular joint) [38]. It usually worsens over time and becomes more accentuated under pressure on the affected area. Pain may also disturb sleep, and its exacerbation during mastication may limit food intake. During the clinical examination, swollen, reddened soft tissue above and around a tooth is found (Figure 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Extraoral photo of recurrent fluctuant cheek swelling with 15 mm of indurated swelling and erythema at the inferior mandibular border, which the article attributes to a dentoalveolar abscess arising from pericoronitis of an erupting first molar. Facially spreading abscess is a recognized complication of pericoronitis; pericoronitis of a first molar (rather than a third molar) makes this a variant presentation. B: Intraoral photograph shows a tender-looking abscess with pericoronal swelling and erythema adjacent to the erupting mandibular molar, explicitly captioned as an intraoral abscess near the right mandibular primary second molar in a case of pericoronitis of an erupting first molar. Involvement of a first/deciduous-region molar rather than a third molar makes the presentation a recognized variant.
panels.attribution_text: Kawashima et al. Dentoalveolar Abscess Caused by Pericoronitis of an Erupting First Molar.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2025. doi:10.3390/diagnostics15121531. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: The cheek abscess recurred 3 weeks later when the patient bumped her cheek. There was no spontaneous pain, fever, or trismus; however, 15 mm of swelling and redness were observed at the inferior border of the mandible. Additionally, an intraoral abscess was found near the right mandibular primary second molar (A,B). Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) was obtained for a more detailed examination.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: Axial CBCT slice showing the osteolytic alveolar bone defect attributed by the article title and caption to pericoronitis of an erupting first molar; disease-focused title plus specific captioned manifestation supports pericoronitis attribution. B: Axial CBCT slice through the right mandible showing the bone defect of the dentoalveolar abscess secondary to pericoronitis; same captioned finding as panel A. C: Axial CBCT slice demonstrating the radiolucent alveolar bone defect around the erupting first molar caused by pericoronitis. D: Axial CBCT slice showing the osteolytic defect/abscess cavity adjacent to the erupting mandibular first molar, attributed to pericoronitis by the article title and caption. E: Axial CBCT slice of the right mandible showing the pericoronitis-related dentoalveolar abscess with alveolar bone destruction. F: Axial CBCT slice showing the radiolucent alveolar bone defect around the erupting first molar...
panels.attribution_text: Kawashima et al. Dentoalveolar Abscess Caused by Pericoronitis of an Erupting First Molar.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2025. doi:10.3390/diagnostics15121531. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: CBCT revealed an alveolar bone defect around the right mandibular first molar, confirming the diagnosis of a dentoalveolar abscess (A–G). In cooperation with the oral surgery department, surgical procedures were performed the next day. The gingival sulcus was incised, and the thinned alveolar bone and surrounding granulation tissue were removed. Antibiotic-containing gauze was placed, and the wound was sutured. Antibiotics and painkillers were prescribed, and the gauze was removed 3 days later. The pain was under control without the use of painkillers, and the redness, induration, and swelling were showing signs of amelioration. No purulent discharge was observed from the wound.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Frontal photograph of the 7-year-old patient with visible right cheek swelling; article title attributes the dentoalveolar abscess to pericoronitis of an erupting first molar, but the facial swelling itself is a secondary sign, so confidence is moderate. B: Lateral photograph showing the swollen, slightly erythematous right cheek described in the caption; manifestation is secondary to the pericoronitis-attributed abscess, hence moderate confidence. C: Intraoral frontal photograph directly shows the erupting right mandibular first molar with painful, inflamed surrounding gingiva — the pericoronal inflammation of pericoronitis confirmed by the article title. D: Lateral intraoral view of the erupting right mandibular first molar with inflamed pericoronal tissue, matching the captioned pericoronitis finding.
panels.attribution_text: Kawashima et al. Dentoalveolar Abscess Caused by Pericoronitis of an Erupting First Molar.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2025. doi:10.3390/diagnostics15121531. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Facial and intraoral photographs at the initial visit. A girl aged 7 years and 3 months was referred to our hospital with a chief complaint of swelling in the right cheek region. She had felt pain in this region a month earlier and was prescribed antibiotics, which alleviated the symptoms. Ten days before her presentation, the swelling recurred and did not improve with antibiotics. She experienced trismus and pain; therefore, she visited the pediatric department of a general hospital, where ultrasonography detected an accumulation of pus in the right cheek region. The doctor determined that a surgical approach was required, so she was referred to our hospital. Her right cheek was swollen and painful to the touch (A,B). Her maximal mouth opening was 1.5 fingers wide and her body temperature was 36.9 °C, indicating a slight fever. Intraoral examination detected an erupting right mandibular first molar surrounded by painful gingiva (C,D). There was neither percussion pain nor drainage. The patient had no relevant medical and family history.
